title: Count Paths in a Grid with Obstacles
directAnswer: Count the ways to walk from the top-left to the bottom-right of an m×n grid, moving only right or down, where some cells are blocked. It's a grid DP: dp[i][j] = number of paths reaching cell (i, j). A blocked cell has 0 paths; otherwise dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j] + dp[i][j-1] (paths arriving from above plus from the left). Seed dp[0][0] = 1 only if the start is free. O(m·n) time, reducible to O(n) space. The trap is an obstacle on the start or in the first row/column — it zeroes out everything downstream of it.

remember.pattern: Grid DP — paths into a cell = paths from above + paths from the left
remember.formula:
if grid[i][j] is blocked: dp[i][j] = 0
elif i == 0 and j == 0: dp[i][j] = 1
else: dp[i][j] = (i>0 ? dp[i-1][j] : 0) + (j>0 ? dp[i][j-1] : 0)
answer = dp[m-1][n-1]
rules: Moves are **right or down only** — so any path into `(i, j)` arrives from `(i-1, j)` (above) or `(i, j-1)` (left).
A **blocked** cell contributes 0 paths; its `dp` is forced to 0 and it passes nothing on.
Seed the start: `dp[0][0] = 1` only if `(0, 0)` is free — a blocked start means **zero** total paths.
First row / first column have a **single** incoming direction; an obstacle there zeroes every cell after it along that line.
Each row depends only on the row above and the cell to the left, so you can compress to **one rolling row** → O(n) space.
whenToUse: Count (not find) the lattice paths in a grid with right/down (or monotone) moves
Cells or edges can be blocked and you must route around them
A DAG of grid cells where each cell's value sums its predecessors
Combinatorial path counting that obstacles make non-closed-form
antiSignals: No obstacles and you just need the count → closed form C(m+n-2, m-1), no DP
You can move in 4 directions / revisit cells → it's a graph traversal, not a DAG DP
You need the shortest or minimum-cost path → BFS / Dijkstra / min-path-sum DP, not counting
Path count overflows → use a big integer or take a modulus
remember.takeaway: Count Paths with Obstacles is the entry-level grid DP: every cell sums the paths from above and from the left, a blocked cell is a hard 0, and the start must be free to count at all. Watch the first row and column — one obstacle there cuts off everything downstream. The same dp underlies Unique Paths, Minimum Path Sum, and Dungeon Game.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you set up dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j] + dp[i][j-1], force blocked cells to 0, seed the start correctly, and handle obstacles in the first row/column that zero out the rest of that line.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Hard-coding dp[0][0] = 1 without checking the start is free, initializing the whole first row/column to 1 ignoring obstacles, or counting a blocked cell as passable.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: State the move constraint that gives the recurrence (right/down → from above or left), explain why a blocked first-row cell zeroes everything after it, then offer the O(n) rolling-row compression and note the no-obstacle closed form.

problemStatement:
You are given an `m × n` integer grid where `grid[i][j] = 0` means the cell is free and `grid[i][j] = 1` means it is blocked by an obstacle.

A robot starts at the **top-left** cell `(0, 0)` and wants to reach the **bottom-right** cell `(m-1, n-1)`. It can move only **right** or **down** at each step, and it cannot enter a blocked cell.

Return the ***number of distinct paths*** the robot can take. If the start or destination is blocked, the answer is `0`.
constraints: Moves are restricted to right and down
The path count can be large but fits in a 64-bit integer for these bounds
understanding: Think of each free cell as a node that can be reached from the cell directly above it or directly to its left, since those are the only moves that land on it. The number of ways to reach a cell is therefore the sum of the ways to reach those two predecessors. Blocked cells are dead — zero ways in, zero ways out. Counting bottom-up from the start fills the grid so the bottom-right cell holds the total number of obstacle-free right/down paths.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Which moves are allowed?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Only right and down. That monotonicity is what makes it a clean DAG DP — a cell's only predecessors are above and to the left, so there are no cycles.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What if the start or end cell is blocked?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Then there are zero paths. A blocked start makes dp[0][0] = 0, which propagates; a blocked end makes dp[m-1][n-1] = 0 directly.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can a path revisit a cell?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No — with only right/down moves you always make progress toward the corner, so cells are never revisited. That's why it's a counting DP, not a search.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Could the count overflow?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: For 100×100 the count can be astronomically large in theory, but the obstacle version stays within 64-bit for the given bounds. If asked, I'd switch to a big integer or a modulus.

examples.explanation: The obstacle at the center forces the two routes: right→right→down→down and down→down→right→right.
The only path is down then right; the obstacle at (0,1) blocks the right-first route.
The start is blocked, so no path can even begin — zero ways.

diagrams.title: Picking the right approach
diagrams.caption: The decision tree to run before writing code. 'Count right/down paths with obstacles' lands on the grid DP.

approaches.name: Brute Force — Recursion Over Right/Down Choices
approaches.whenToMention: Say this first to establish the 'paths = from above + from left' recurrence and the obstacle/boundary rules, then flag the exponential branching.
hints: At each free cell you can go right or down. How many ways reach a given cell? Sum the ways that reach the cells you could have stepped from.
Define solve(i, j) = number of paths from the start to cell (i, j). It comes from the cell above and the cell to the left.
Base cases: a blocked cell has 0 paths; the start (0,0) has 1 if free. Out-of-bounds predecessors contribute 0.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each cell branches into its two predecessors and those branches overlap heavily; the unmemoized tree is exponential in m + n. Recursion depth is O(m + n).
approaches.explanation:
Define `solve(i, j)` = the number of distinct right/down paths from the start `(0, 0)` to cell `(i, j)`.

- If `(i, j)` is blocked, no path can be on it → 0.
- If `(i, j)` is the start and it's free → 1 (the empty path).
- Otherwise sum the paths arriving from the only two cells you could have stepped from: above `solve(i-1, j)` (if `i > 0`) and left `solve(i, j-1)` (if `j > 0`).

**Why the recurrence sums exactly two predecessors.** The robot moves only right or down, so the last step onto `(i, j)` was either a downward step from `(i-1, j)` or a rightward step from `(i, j-1)`. Every path to `(i, j)` ends with one of those two steps, and the two sets are disjoint (they differ in the final move), so the count is the sum of the counts to those predecessors. This 'sum the ways into my predecessors' is the defining shape of a counting DP on a DAG.

**Why blocked cells are a hard zero.** A blocked cell can never be stood on, so zero paths reach it and it forwards zero to its successors. Returning 0 there automatically routes the count around obstacles — no special-casing of neighbours needed.

**Why boundaries contribute 0, not 1.** A cell in the top row has no cell above it; a cell in the left column has none to its left. Treating those missing predecessors as 0 (rather than skipping the base case) keeps the recurrence uniform. Only the start seeds a 1.

**Why we don't ship this.** `solve(i-1, j)` and `solve(i, j-1)` both recurse into `solve(i-1, j-1)`, and so on, so the same cell is recomputed exponentially often. Caching `solve(i, j)` collapses it to `O(m·n)`.
approaches.insight: The state is the cell `(i, j)` and the recursion revisits the same cell through many path prefixes. A 2-D grid state plus exponential overlap is the textbook signal for an O(m·n) DP.

Sum the two predecessors — these branches overlap, which is why we cache next.

edgeCases.behavior: Start equals end and is free → 1 path.

pitfalls: Returning 1 for out-of-bounds predecessors instead of 0 — over-counts along the borders.
Forgetting the obstacle check before the start check — a blocked start would wrongly return 1.
Skipping this approach — the 'sum of two predecessors' recurrence is what the interviewer wants verbalized.

approaches.name: Top-Down Memoization on (i, j)
approaches.whenToMention: The fix once you name the overlap — 'cache solve(i, j) so each cell is computed once'.
hints: solve(i, j) returns the same count every call. Where can you store it so each cell is computed once?
Use a 2-D memo of size m × n. Mark cells 'uncomputed' with -1 (real counts are ≥ 0), check on entry, store before returning.
There are O(m·n) cells and each does O(1) work → O(m·n) time and space.
approaches.complexityReasoning: There are m·n distinct (i, j) states; each combines two cached sub-results in O(1) → O(m·n) time. The memo is O(m·n); recursion depth is O(m + n) on top.
approaches.explanation:
Keep the 'sum of two predecessors' recurrence but cache `solve(i, j)` so each cell is computed once.

**The mental shift: the count into a cell is fixed.** However the recursion reaches `(i, j)`, the number of paths from the start to that cell is a single value. Caching by `(i, j)` removes all the duplicated subtrees, leaving `O(m·n)` distinct cells each resolved in `O(1)`.

**Sentinel choice.** Initialise the memo to -1 for 'uncomputed' — real path counts are non-negative, and a free start legitimately returns 1, so 0 can't double as 'empty'. Blocked cells return 0 before any caching.

**A language note (Java memo vs Python tabulation).** This recursion nests up to `O(m + n)` deep. For the 100×100 bound that's ~200 — fine in both languages. But for very large grids the depth could approach **Python's default recursion limit of about 1000**, at which point you'd raise the limit with `sys.setrecursionlimit` or, cleaner, switch to the bottom-up table (next approach) that uses no stack at all. Top-down memoization is the natural default in Java; bottom-up is the safer default in Python once grids get tall or wide.
approaches.insight: Standard DP upgrade: the correct recurrence plus a cache keyed on the cell `(i, j)`. The thinking — two predecessors, obstacle = 0, free start = 1 — was done in the brute force.

Cache hit returns the stored count in O(1).

java.line: memo[i][j] = solve(grid, i - 1, j, memo) + solve(grid, i, j - 1, memo);
java.explanation: Store the summed predecessors before returning so the cell is never recomputed.

python.explanation: Caches solve by (i, j) — the natural 2-D memo.

pitfalls: Using 0 as the sentinel — a free start returns 1 and blocked cells return 0, so 0 is a real value; use null/-1.
Checking the start base case before the obstacle guard — a blocked start would wrongly return 1.
Deep recursion in Python on tall/wide grids — tabulation avoids the stack.

approaches.name: Bottom-Up — Grid Table, Rolling Row (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want. Frame it as 'dp[i][j] = up + left, sweep row by row', then compress to one row.
hints: Let dp[i][j] = number of paths to cell (i, j). Fill row by row, left to right, so the cell above and the cell to the left are already done.
Seed dp[0][0] = 1 if the start is free, else 0. A blocked cell sets dp[i][j] = 0; otherwise dp[i][j] = up + left (treat off-grid as 0).
Since row i depends only on row i-1 and the cell to its left, keep a single rolling row of length n → O(n) space. Answer is the last cell.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Filling m·n cells with O(1) work each is O(m·n) time. Each row needs only the previous row's values, so one rolling array of length n gives O(n) space.
approaches.explanation:
Let `dp[i][j]` be the number of right/down paths from the start to cell `(i, j)`. Sweep the grid top to bottom, left to right, so both predecessors are already computed when you reach a cell. The answer is `dp[m-1][n-1]`.

**Seeding the start.** `dp[0][0] = 1` only if `(0, 0)` is free; if the start is blocked it's 0 and the whole grid stays 0. This single check is the most-missed detail — hard-coding `dp[0][0] = 1` reports phantom paths through a blocked start.

**The fill rule.** For every other cell: if it's blocked, `dp[i][j] = 0`; otherwise `dp[i][j] = up + left`, where `up = dp[i-1][j]` (0 if `i == 0`) and `left = dp[i][j-1]` (0 if `j == 0`). Treating off-grid predecessors as 0 makes the first row and first column fall out naturally — each has just one incoming direction.

**Why obstacles in the first row/column are sharp.** In the top row a cell's only predecessor is its left neighbour; once an obstacle sets a cell to 0, every cell to its right inherits `left = 0` and stays 0. The first column behaves the same vertically. Initializing borders to a blanket 1 (a common bug) ignores this and over-counts.

**Why the sweep order is valid.** `dp[i][j]` reads only `dp[i-1][j]` (row above, already filled) and `dp[i][j-1]` (same row, already filled this pass). Top-to-bottom, left-to-right satisfies both — no recursion, so Python's stack limit is irrelevant.

**Space compression.** Because row `i` depends only on row `i-1` and the current row's left cell, a single rolling array of length `n` suffices: when you process cell `j`, `row[j]` still holds the value from the row above (the 'up') and `row[j-1]` holds the freshly updated 'left'. Set `row[j] = 0` for obstacles. That drops space from `O(m·n)` to `O(n)`.

**No-obstacle aside.** Without any blocks the answer is the binomial `C(m+n-2, m-1)` — worth mentioning, but obstacles break the closed form, which is exactly why DP earns its place.
approaches.insight: This is the canonical grid counting DP: each cell sums its in-edges (up + left), a blocked cell is a 0, fill in dependency order, then compress to one row. The same skeleton powers Unique Paths (no obstacles), Minimum Path Sum (min instead of sum), and Dungeon Game (reverse sweep).

dryRun.intro: Rolling row of length 3. Start free → row=[1,?,?]. Obstacle zeroes its cell.

java.line: row[0] = (grid[0][0] == 0) ? 1 : 0;  // seed only if start is free
java.explanation: The start seeds 1 path only when it's not an obstacle — the most common slip.
First row: one incoming direction; an obstacle zeroes everything after it.
First column obstacle cuts off the column below it.

java.line: row[j] = row[j] + row[j - 1]; // up (old row[j]) + left
java.explanation: row[j] still holds the row-above value (up); row[j-1] is the just-updated left.

python.line: row[0] = 1 if grid[0][0] == 0 else 0   # seed only if start is free

python.explanation: First-row propagation halts permanently at an obstacle.

python.line: row[j] = row[j] + row[j - 1]  # up (old row[j]) + left
python.explanation: The rolling-row trick: old value = up, left neighbour = left.

edgeCases.behavior: row[0] seeded to 0 → entire grid stays 0 → answer 0.
No cell below is reachable from above past that row → end cell 0.
Single line of cells; any obstacle blocks the only path → 0, else 1.

pitfalls: Seeding dp[0][0] = 1 without checking the start is free.
Initializing the whole first row/column to 1 — ignores obstacles that should zero the rest of the line.
Adding the left neighbour into a blocked cell instead of forcing it to 0 — leaks paths through walls.

commonMistakes: Seeding the start cell to 1 without checking it's free.
Initializing the entire first row and column to 1, ignoring obstacles there.
Letting a blocked cell still accumulate paths instead of forcing it to 0.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Unconditional start seed
commonMistakesDetailed.why: If grid[0][0] is an obstacle there are zero paths, but hard-coding dp[0][0] = 1 reports phantom routes that start on a wall.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Blanket first row/column = 1
commonMistakesDetailed.why: The first row/column have one incoming direction, so an obstacle there zeroes every later cell on that line. Setting them all to 1 over-counts paths that actually run into a wall.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad: for (int j = 0; j < n; j++) dp[0][j] = 1;   // ignores obstacles in row 0

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Blocked cell still sums predecessors
commonMistakesDetailed.why: If you compute up + left for an obstacle cell, paths leak through the wall and propagate. A blocked cell must be a hard 0 regardless of its neighbours.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad: row[j] = row[j] + row[j - 1]      # runs even when grid[i][j] == 1

followupVariations.title: Unique Paths
followupVariations.hint: No obstacles — same DP, or the closed form C(m+n-2, m-1).

followupVariations.title: Minimum Path Sum
followupVariations.hint: Same grid skeleton, but take min of up/left and add the cell's cost instead of summing counts.

followupVariations.title: Dungeon Game
followupVariations.hint: Right/down grid DP filled in reverse — track minimum health needed to survive.

followupVariations.title: Unique Paths III
followupVariations.hint: Must visit every free cell with 4-directional moves — switches to backtracking, not a simple DP.

patternNote: Canonical grid counting DP on a right/down DAG. Recognise it when you count monotone lattice paths and cells can be blocked: each free cell sums the paths from above and from the left, a blocked cell is 0, and the free start seeds 1. Compress to one rolling row. Same skeleton as Unique Paths, Minimum Path Sum, and Dungeon Game.
